final_claim.narrative:
All 9 triangles incident to the target set closed within the 800-unit threshold (fraction_closed = 1.0) with a median closing lag of only 181 units — roughly a quarter of the allowed delta, so closures track their supporting wedges tightly rather than merely coexisting in the log (step_02, step_03). Direct verification confirms genuine temporal ordering: for {64, 102, 1152} the wedge legs land at 23904 and 24502 and the closing 64->102 edge fires at 24554, 52 units later (step_09, step_08); the 18-42 closing edge likewise exists as a single directed event (step_12).

The main confounders fail. (1) Volume: these nodes are extremely quiet, 2-5 events each with no repeats, and none appear in the top-10 active list (step_05, step_04) — the perfect closure rate cannot be manufactured by sheer event density. (2) Popularity/hub artefact: the wedge centres are low-degree, e.g. node 378 has just 3 neighbours (step_13), so shared contacts are not incidental co-occurrence at a hub. (3) Baseline: the busiest nodes in the identical window yield 91 triangles but only 15.4% prompt closure and a median lag of 2427 units (step_07) — a 13x worse lag, establishing that prompt closure is not a background property of this window. (4) Specificity in time: the same node set produces zero triangles in the preceding window [10000, 22552] (step_06), so the pattern is localised to the queried interval rather than a standing structural feature.

One qualification lowering confidence from certainty: the closures are distributed across the window (t_close from 24554 to 32966) with activity peaking in two clusters (step_14), so this reads as a sustained prompt-closure regime rather than one tightly synchronised burst. The count of 9 triangles is also modest. The mechanism criterion — closing interactions promptly following their supporting interactions — is nonetheless clearly met.
